South Carolina had not elected a Democrat to the U.S. Senate since 1998, when Fritz Hollings won his final term, and Trump carried the state by nearly 18 points in 2024, according to Associated Press election data. Andrews, a Democratic pediatrician who had never held elected office before, defeated appointed Sen. Darline Graham, R-S.C., the sister of the late Sen. Lindsey Graham, by nearly five points.

Graham had Trump’s endorsement and the president also helped her with late campaign appearances on the trail. She had been appointed to serve out her brother’s term after his death, then won the Republican nomination for a full six-year term.

Andrews’ win broke a nearly three-decade Republican hold on the state’s Senate seat and became a rare moment when a Trump-backed candidate lost in a state Republicans had long counted on.

Sen. Darline Graham, R-S.C., and Democratic challenger Annie Andrews face off during a South Carolina U.S. Senate debate in Columbia on Oct. 11, 2026. Andrews went on to defeat Graham, ending a nearly three-decade Republican hold on the seat. (Courtesy: SCETV).

It has been revealed that kansas had not sent a Democrat to the U.S. Senate since 1932, when George McGill won a full term. Hamilton, a Democrat and the founding pastor of a large United Methodist church, defeated first-term Sen. Roger Marshall, R-Kan., in a state Trump carried by 16 points in 2024, according to election data from the Associated Press.

The Kansas race was long viewed as a Republican hold, but major election forecasters moved it into toss-up territory late in the campaign as Marshall faced scrutiny over his residency and lawsuits his former medical practice filed against patients.

Trump and Vice President JD Vance both campaigned for Marshall, and Republican-aligned groups spent heavily to keep the seat, including more than $26 million committed to ads supporting him after the August primary — more than was spent on Marshall during his first race in 2020, according to AdImpact data cited by the Associated Press.

Hamilton’s win ended a 94-year Republican Senate streak.

According to recent reports, sen. Roger Marshall, R-Kan., left, and Democratic challenger Adam Hamilton, who became the first Democrat elected to the U.S. Senate from Kansas since 1932. (Getty Images).

Sources indicate that democrat J.D. Ford defeated three-term Rep. Victoria Spartz, R-Ind., in Indiana’s 5th Congressional District, which Trump carried by about 17 points, according to Associated Press election results from 2024. Spartz had won re-election there by 18.6 points in 2024, and the district had not elected a Democrat since 1990, when Jim Jontz won.

According to recent reports, ford, a Democratic state senator, won 51.7% to Spartz’s 48.3%, according to the Associated Press results after the midterms. His victory was the only Indiana House seat to change parties, making it a sharp reversal in a state that Trump carried by 19 points statewide in 2024.

The Associated Press has yet to formally call the race with 99% of the vote counted so far.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Welcome to Foreign Policy’s Africa Brief.

The highlights this week: Ukraine attacks Russian vessels in Libya in “response to Russia’s war,” Gambia wins a landmark case at the International Court of Justice, and African nations respond to a disappointing United Nations climate summit.

Welcome to Foreign Policy’s Africa Brief.

The highlights this week: Ukraine attacks Russian vessels in Libya in “response to Russia’s war,” Gambia wins a landmark case at the International Court of Justice, and African nations respond to a disappointing United Nations climate summit.

According to recent reports, kyiv claimed responsibility on Monday for a recent attack on two Russian vessels off the coast of Libya, including the corvette Merkury, one of Russia’s newest warships. The vessels had been docked at the Benghazi naval base when the attack occurred on Sunday.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky has described the operation as “exemplary” and noted that it was in “response to Russia’s war.”.

Yet security experts warn that conducting drone strikes within a region that is not involved in the Russia-Ukraine war could set a dangerous precedent, especially as they fear Africa is becoming a proxy theater in the conflict.

According to recent reports, the United Nations mission in Libya, known as UNSMIL, has called for “an immediate, independent and transparent investigation” into the drone strikes. “Libya cannot afford, and must not become, a battleground for foreign conflicts,” UNSMIL wrote on X.

Recent findings suggest that kyiv has confirmed that seven Ukrainian-made naval drones had been released from a “mothership” in the region, though it did not clarify how they were transported there. Some unverified Libyan sources have alleged that Tripoli’s U.N.-recognized government may have aided Ukraine, which Tripoli strongly denied.

Recent findings suggest that both of Libya’s rival administrations—the government in Tripoli, led by Prime Minister Abdul Hamid Dbeibah, and a Russia-backed government based in Benghazi, controlled by Gen. Khalifa Haftar—have denounced the attacks.

Following the 2024 fall of the Assad regime in Syria, where Russia operates a naval base, Moscow has sought alternative military footprints in Africa, including by pursuing airbases in eastern Libya. Syria served as a logistical hub for transferring troops and arms to landlocked Sahel nations, where Russia’s mercenary Africa Corps helps fight jihadists.

With Syria growing closer to the United States and Europe, Libya now serves as that hub, explained Ulf Laessing, the head of the Syria/Iraq program at the Konrad-Adenauer-Stiftung and the author of Understanding Libya Since Gaddafi.

Sources indicate that “Ukraine is trying to hit Russia wherever they can. It’s difficult for Ukraine to hit Russian targets where the Africa Corps is based in the Sahel,” Laessing remarked. “It’s more efficient and easier to do it where Russia is basically bringing goods.”.

Zain Hussain, a researcher at the Stockholm International Peace Research Institute, stated that “through this attack, Ukraine is showing that it can target Russia’s geopolitical interests as well as fighting a war with Russia at home.”.

According to recent reports, the strikes come amid increasing concern that the war in Ukraine is spreading to other African countries. Ukrainian drone specialists have been deployed to Libya, Mali, and Sudan, according to a September CNN report. A source also told CNN that troops from Chad, Niger, and Burkina Faso had traveled to Mali to receive drone training from Ukrainian soldiers, though several experts told me that the evidence for this is speculative at best.

Meanwhile, in the Sahel, multiple media reports have accused Ukraine of supporting and training northern Mali’s Tuareg separatists in recent years as a means of wearing down Russian forces there.

Experts suspect Ukrainian drone assistance in the Tuareg ambush that killed dozens of Russian Wagner mercenaries and Malian soldiers in 2024. At the time, Andriy Yusov, a spokesperson for Ukrainian military intelligence, said that the rebels had been given the “necessary” information to carry out the attacks. Yusov’s comments prompted Mali to sever relations with Ukraine, accusing Kyiv of supporting a “barbaric” attack by terrorists.

Recent findings suggest that analysts also suspected Ukrainian involvement in the brief insurgent takeover of Mali’s strategic town of Kidal earlier this year by Tuareg and al Qaeda-linked jihadists. Ukraine’s Foreign Ministry has officially rejected the allegations.

Ukraine’s latest attacks are unlikely to disrupt eastern Libya’s ties with Russia, Laessing noted, especially as Moscow needs “a country on the way to the Sahel.” Still, they add a layer of complexity to long-standing violence and drone warfare in Sahelian nations, said Virginie Baudais, the director of the Stockholm International Peace Research Institute’s Sahel and West Africa program.

As Baudais put it, the “internationalization of the conflict” in the Sahel will only contribute to “the escalation of violence, with the highest cost for civilian populations.”.

Monday, Nov. 23, to Friday, Nov. 27: The Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention’s public health conference is held in Addis Ababa, Ethiopia.

Industry observers note that friday, Nov. 27: The deadline for councils in South Africa to elect their leaders.

Recent findings suggest that somalia-UAE rift. Last week, Somalia expelled the United Arab Emirates’ ambassador and recalled its own envoy from Abu Dhabi, citing ​violations of the country’s sovereignty that amounted to an “open invasion.”.

The dispute stems from growing Emirati ties with Ethiopia and the Somalian breakaway regions of Somaliland and Puntland. Somali President Hassan Sheikh Mohamud also accused the UAE of having played a role in Israel’s recognition of Somaliland last December in a statement to Somalian state news agency SONNA.

Industry observers note that the UAE’s state-owned DP World and its subsidiaries operate ports in those breakaway regions. They have expanded the Berbera port in Somaliland and are developing a road corridor connecting it to landlocked Ethiopia. In January 2024, Addis Ababa signed a memorandum of understanding to eventually recognize Somaliland’s independence in exchange for naval and commercial access to Berbera.

A Latest York Times report using satellite imagery recently found that the UAE has turned airports in Berbera and Bosaso, a city in Puntland, into military facilities.

In response to Somalia’s latest move, the UAE said its embassy in Somalia had been closed since January, after Mogadishu canceled bilateral agreements, and it strongly denounced the “escalatory and hostile approach” by the Somali government amid the latest diplomatic spat.

In a recent development, ICJ ruling. Gambia, the smallest nation in mainland Africa, won a landmark case last week when the International Court of Justice (ICJ) ruled that Myanmar committed genocide in its 2017 military campaign that killed at least 10,000 members of the Rohingya Muslim minority community and displaced more than 700,000 into neighboring Bangladesh.

Recent findings suggest that A Muslim-majority nation, Gambia brought the case to the court in 2019. Now, the ruling has possible implications for South Africa’s ICJ genocide case against Israel for its operations in Gaza.

Both Myanmar and Israel have defended their actions as counterinsurgency operations. But in its decision, the court considered a pattern of mass killings, the razing of homes, and forced exodus. That finding “gives South Africa more avenues ​to argue for genocide” in Gaza, Israeli legal expert Yuval Shany told Reuters.

Recent findings suggest that COP31’s failures. This year’s U.N. climate summit, known as COP31, in Turkey ended on Sunday without an agreement after references to phasing out fossil fuels were removed from the draft text. Despite being the most attended COP to date, some observers have called it the “worst” one ever.

At the summit, African delegations voiced discontent with financial commitments for climate adaptation. Wealthier nations pledged only $50 million in total to the climate adaptation fund, far short of the $300 million annual target. They also largely offered loans rather than grants. The United States, the United Kingdom, Canada, France, Italy, and Australia did not make any funding commitments.

Africa, which is home to 17 percent of the world’s population, is responsible for just 4 percent of global carbon emissions. Yet the continent faces disproportionate impacts from climate change.

The African Group of Negotiators (AGN), chaired by Ghana, rejected attempts to weaken both finance targets and the Paris Agreement’s goal of limiting warming to 1.5 degrees Celsius. It said that the debate on fossil fuels had “overshadowed” broken promises on adaptation finance.

Recent findings suggest that “Those who were arguing about whether we should get fossil fuels in the cover decision or not were producers, exporters, importers and users of fossil fuels,” AGN chair Antwi-Boasiako Amoah remarked. “It was hypocrisy.”.

Industry observers note that AFCON verdict. Senegal was reinstated as the 2025 Africa Cup of Nations champion in a much-anticipated ruling by the Court of Arbitration for Sport on Tuesday.

Senegal initially won the final against Morocco 1-0 in extra time in January. Two months later, however, the Confederation of African Football (CAF) stripped the country of its title, awarding it to Morocco because Senegalese players temporarily walked off the pitch to protest refereeing decisions.

The court overturned CAF’s decision because the match was allowed to conclude. “By blowing his whistle to restart play, the Referee considered that the conditions for resuming the match had been met,” the court stated in a statement. Morocco prepares to appeal the decision.

Recent findings suggest that sudanese excavations. Last week, archaeologists unearthed the original floor of the largest medieval church in Nubia, in northern Sudan’s ancient city of Old Dongola. It was part of Makuria, one of three Christian Nubian kingdoms that existed from the sixth to 16th centuries.

The church was first discovered in 2021, but excavations were suspended two years later following the outbreak of Sudan’s civil war. Operations resumed last year in the abandoned city, which has managed to escape widespread destruction from the conflict so far.

UNESCO estimated that more than 100 cultural sites have been damaged, looted, or destroyed since fighting began in Sudan in April 2023.

These accounts have posted artificial intelligence-generated content and videos from elsewhere in Africa, including Somalia, as supposed evidence of persecution in Nigeria.

As the creators “continue to spread misinformation, concerns are growing that their online influence could have real-world consequences,” Olaoye writes. “Campaigns like these can deepen ethno-religious fault lines, shape political decisions, and fuel reprisal attacks.”.

AI bioweapons. In Rest of World, Danai Nesta Kupemba reports on researchers at a small AI lab in Ghana who “jailbroke” their own drug-discovery AI model, which allowed them to quickly design thousands of toxic molecules, to warn about the potential for AI bioweapons misuse.

“Scholars have long warned about AI’s bioweapons threat, but it is only recently that AI systems have truly outperformed Ph.D.-level biologists,” Kupemba writes.

It has been revealed that IVO H. DAALDER is Senior Fellow at Harvard’s Belfer Center for Science and International Affairs. He served as U.S. Ambassador to NATO from 2009 to 2013.

According to recent reports, JAMES M. LINDSAY is Mary and David Boies Distinguished Senior Fellow in U.S. Foreign Policy at the Council on Foreign Relations.

How to Defuse Looming Threats to U.S. National Security.

Ivo H. Daalder and James M. Lindsay.

It has been revealed that democrats won a historic victory in the U.S. midterm elections by running on a key voter concern: affordability. They promised to lower gas and diesel prices, curb electricity and water bills, and cut borrowing costs. Now voters expect results.

Industry observers note that making progress will not be easy, given that the affordability crisis is inextricably linked to a set of thorny policy concerns. Soaring gas and diesel prices stem from wars in Europe and the Middle East that have overextended the United States and provided China, Iran, North Korea, and Russia openings to exploit. Rising electricity and water bills are driven by the growing number of data centers powering an artificial intelligence revolution that is nearing a point of no return, when machines improve faster than humans can understand or control. And higher prices and borrowing costs are the result of an unsustainable U.S. national debt, now above $40 trillion, that requires exorbitant interest payments and has foreign governments questioning the safety of the dollar and U.S. Treasury bonds.

Industry observers note that these problems not only strain Americans’ pocketbooks but also threaten the security and prosperity of the United States—and the world. If Beijing and Moscow try to take advantage of a weakened United States by escalating simultaneously in Taiwan and eastern Europe, those moves could be the first steps toward World War III. If AI escapes the bounds of human control, no one will be safe. And if the national debt continues to soar, Washington could trigger a fiscal crisis that devastates the American economy and leaves the United States far less able to meet the challenges it faces overseas.

Recent findings suggest that action to address the United States’ problems therefore cannot wait. But politics may stand in the way. The White House is more likely to obstruct than to cooperate with congressional Democrats over the next two years, as President Donald Trump’s appointment of the pugilistic Stephen Miller as the latest White House chief of staff underscores. Moreover, one electoral victory did not erase the country’s deep partisan and policy divisions. Going into the 2028 presidential election, Republicans know that a successful Democratic Congress would endanger their chances of keeping the White House. Trump and congressional Republicans, therefore, have considerable motivation to derail Democratic prepares.

Democrats are not without options, however. They can pursue legislation, seeking cross-party collaboration when possible and pushing ahead even in the face of presidential vetoes. Sometimes it is the president, not Congress, who blinks. When he doesn’t, voters will know who stood in the way. Democrats can also use public hearings and the investigative powers of Congress to shed light on the threats facing the country and to build a case for change—much as the Fulbright hearings did during the Vietnam War and the Church Committee did to highlight Cold War–era intelligence abuses. They can put the defense secretary and military commanders, AI executives, and Treasury and budget officials under oath to account for how they prosecuted the Iran war, raced ahead on AI without adequate safeguards, and exploded the deficit. They can also call on economists, scientists, and strategists to explain how to steer the country away from peril.

Congressional efforts may not be enough to meaningfully change Trump’s policies. But the risks of major war, unconstrained AI, and eroding economic competitiveness are too great to wait two more years to address. These problems, and the affordability crisis they have generated, will only get worse. If Democrats in Congress do not start advancing a serious agenda to address them now, these dangers may become impossible to contain.

It has been revealed that the first order of the upcoming Congress’s business should be to end the Iran war. Operation Epic Fury has sent energy prices soaring and put freedom of navigation at risk. It has also highlighted the United States’ vulnerabilities in ways that could prove dangerous—and costly—in the years ahead. Iranian missiles and drones wreaked havoc on American military bases in the Persian Gulf. U.S. efforts to defeat these attacks depleted supplies of critical munitions, showing that the U.S. military has become overly reliant on very expensive, hard-to-produce high-tech weapons. The economic, diplomatic, military, and intelligence support that China and Russia have provided Iran revealed the extent to which autocracies are cooperating to stretch U.S. capabilities and undermine American power. The U.S. Navy is effectively bottled up in the Arabian Sea, limiting its presence in the Atlantic and Pacific. In theory, U.S. allies could help fill the gaps, but Trump’s decision to launch the war without consulting them and his adversarial attitude toward them have strained those relationships, weakening deterrence of a Russia and China bent on securing strategic advantage.

According to recent reports, perceptions of weakness, even when they are wrong, are often why wars begin. Moscow and Beijing might see the next two years as a window of opportunity. Europe and Japan are rearming, but that buildup will take years. The American military is stretched thin, and political divisions make decisive action difficult. Together this could be an invitation for U.S. adversaries to engage in aggression in Europe and Asia. Russia is already pursuing a shadow war against NATO and could test the alliance’s unity further by probing the Baltic states. China could impose a blockade on Taiwan. It is not difficult to see how, if Moscow and Beijing take these steps in concert, the resulting conflicts could escalate into a global war.

In a recent development, the upcoming Congress will have limited ability to forestall these events. The U.S. Constitution puts much of diplomacy beyond the reach of the legislature; only the president decides when to negotiate, what to discuss, and with whom. But Congress does have tools to wield. If the Trump administration remains in a standoff with the Iranian regime when Democrats take control in January, Congress should immediately invoke the War Powers Resolution to pass binding legislation demanding that Trump either secure congressional authorization for the war or end it. Congress can also use its power of the purse to condition or halt further spending on the war, preferably as part of must-pass legislation, such as a defense appropriations bill, to avoid a potential Senate filibuster. Trump would likely veto any such legislation, and Congress has a poor record on overriding presidential vetoes. But challenging a war that Americans clearly oppose would fulfill the promise Democrats made on the campaign trail, reduce the likelihood that Trump would escalate in dangerous ways, and mark a step forward in Congress’s reclamation of its war powers.

There is more the Democratic Congress can do to lower the risks of global conflict, too. It can start by taking a stronger line on Russia. Moscow has repaid Trump’s conciliatory policies—including his waiving of sanctions Congress authorized earlier this year with the bipartisan Lindsay O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act—with aid to Tehran and an intensified war on Ukraine. Only greater pressure can force the Kremlin to stand down. Congress should amend the Graham Act to give itself the right to review and overturn any presidential waivers of sanctions mandated under the law. It should also reaffirm the current ban on energy purchases from Russia and prohibit the administration from using government funds to follow through on its proposal to restart Russian gas and oil exports to Europe through a U.S. intermediary. Congress should resume military aid to Ukraine, ensure the availability of Starshield communications to Ukrainian forces, and refuse to fund any reduction in the permanent U.S. military presence in Europe or Asia that it has not approved itself.

Finally, to help dissuade China from threatening Taiwan, Congress should use defense spending bills to speed up the sale of arms to Taiwan. And Congress should legally codify the 1982 Six Assurances, which include a promise by Washington not to consult Beijing on arms sales to Taiwan. Many of these measures could garner sufficient Republican support to pass with veto-proof majorities, forcing Trump’s hand.

According to recent reports, additionally, Congress should use its oversight powers to assess the vulnerabilities that the Iran war has revealed. It should evaluate whether the U.S. intelligence agencies and the Pentagon adequately anticipated Iran’s response to U.S. attacks, the scale and causes of the shortages of high-tech weapons, and the risks that AI-aided drone warfare poses to U.S. overseas bases. Congress can also review the extent of Chinese and Russian support for Iran; assess NATO’s defenses against Russia, including its response to the escalating shadow war; determine U.S. readiness for Chinese efforts to coerce Taiwan; and evaluate proposals to make Pentagon acquisition more flexible and less expensive. An essential step toward enhancing U.S. deterrence is to identify what is broken in the U.S. defense posture and what needs to be fixed.

Industry observers note that the newly introduced Congress will also need to rein in the AI industry. Opposition to AI data centers and other infrastructure galvanized voters in the midterms. Across the country, 46 of 47 ballot measures passed, placing new restrictions on new data centers, which have brought rising power and water bills and explosive land costs. Many Americans fear what AI will do to jobs today and for the next generation. They distrust the tech executives who control it and question who will truly benefit from its development.

It has been revealed that those concerns are justified. AI is advancing with increasing speed and introducing unknown risks. Five months ago, AI generated one percent of Anthropic’s research and development; today, it accounts for more than a quarter. Lab leaders predict that AI will become self-generating within a year. That is a scary prospect, not only for displaced computer scientists but also for society at large. AI could pose an existential threat to global computer networks; rogue AI agents have already colluded to evade human control. Leading firms have warned of even greater dangers. Alphabet stated recently that its products could lead to “severe or catastrophic security and societal incidents,” and Anthropic has cited “catastrophic or existential risks to humanity.”.

Sources indicate that AI also poses profound national security challenges for the United States. The Trump administration and the tech industry have invoked an innovation race with China as a reason not to regulate the technology. That race is real, but many of the most important stages are not the ones Washington is fixating on. They are also ones Beijing is winning. Perhaps U.S. firms will be the first to develop artificial general intelligence. But in the meantime, the rest of the world and many U.S. companies are adopting Chinese open-weight AI models. Alibaba’s Qwen model now accounts for more than half of all open-source model downloads worldwide. As cheap, easy-to-adapt Chinese models become the global default, Beijing gains leverage over the digital infrastructure on which other countries’ economies and militaries will run. The companies that build these models are legally bound to cooperate with Chinese intelligence services. And because these models spread with few safeguards, they are easier to turn to malicious use.

It has been revealed that meanwhile, AI is transforming war. Autonomous weapons are essential to Ukraine’s defense against a superior military, shooting down long-range drones and targeting Russian forces, supply lines, and strategic industries. This year, the Pentagon quietly revised its doctrine to let AI select and initiate strikes while humans merely monitor, which risks errors and escalation at a speed no human can catch. And as AI lowers the barriers to entry for launching cyberattacks and developing fresh biological weapons, every country is in danger.

According to recent reports, the Trump administration is clearly reluctant to address any of these threats. It is beholden to figures such as Jensen Huang, Elon Musk, and Mark Zuckerburg who have wanted to keep the AI industry unregulated and unconstrained. Huang and Nvidia, the firm he led, had long pushed the administration to relax U.S. export controls that restricted the sale of AI chips to China and other countries; the firm’s current scandal has revealed just how loose those restrictions had become. Now, the administration wants China to report serious AI-related incidents through a new bilateral channel yet opposes requiring American companies to do the same. Given how rapidly AI is advancing, Congress cannot afford to stand idly by. There is a slew of legislative proposals already circulating, many of them with bipartisan support, that would require incident reporting, auditors in AI labs, and mandatory safety testing before deployment. Other AI industry leaders, such as Anthropic’s Dario Amodei and Alphabet’s Demis Hassabis, have supported these ideas, but the Trump administration has ignored them, asking instead for the industry to police itself.

Finding the right regulations and safety mechanisms, and then codifying them in legislation, will take time. In the meantime, Congress should use its convening power to seek input from industry leaders, experts, and the public about how this technology can be controlled. The leaders of frontier AI labs should be asked, under oath, to explain not just the upside of AI but also its risks. Elon Musk, for example, told The Economist this summer that within ten years, work will be “optional” because of AI—but he has also remarked there is a ten to 20 percent chance that AI will lead to the extinction of humanity. He and others who share this belief should be forced to justify why this risk is acceptable and why tech leaders are the ones to decide on behalf of humanity. They should also explain what it would take to reduce the ten to 20 percent chance to zero.

Public hearings that expose both the dangers and the opportunities of AI will make it easier to galvanize action to harness the technology’s promise safely while preventing the worst possible outcomes. And Congress has some levers it can pull now to address threats to national security. It can use the defense authorization bill to require that humans retain meaningful control over lethal force and to demand an accounting of how AI is reshaping military doctrine. It can also fund efforts to make American models, rather than Chinese ones, the default choice for countries around the world. If legislation takes too long to pass, hearings can at least lay the groundwork for a future administration to act.

Sources indicate that finally, Congress must address threats to the United States’ economic power. With $40 trillion in public debt, an annual budget deficit of $2 trillion, and annual interest payments topping more than $1 trillion, the U.S. economy is living on borrowed time. China and Russia are working to “de-dollarize” their economies by encouraging the use of cryptocurrency and other means of settling international transactions and by creating alternatives to the U.S.-dominated global banking system.

In a recent development, even U.S. allies are reducing their reliance on that system: Norway’s sovereign wealth fund has cut its holding of U.S. dollars, the Dutch and French central banks have pulled their gold holdings from Fresh York, and European Central Bank President Christine Lagarde has called for a “global euro” that would serve as an alternative to the dollar. If the dollar were to lose its status as the world’s premier reserve currency, Washington would be forced to spend even more money servicing the debt than it does now, intensifying the country’s fiscal problems, slowing economic growth while driving up inflation, and diminishing its ability to use economic and financial sanctions to pressure adversaries.

An immediate objective for the Democratic Congress will be to rein in Trump’s tariffs, because they raise prices, unsettle the markets that finance U.S. debt, and make U.S. producers less competitive globally without making a meaningful dent in the deficit. Congress will be operating from a disadvantage. Over the past century, it has delegated to the White House considerable tariff-setting authority, which Trump has eagerly exercised. Clawing back that power will be difficult. Significant disagreement exists among Democrats and between Democrats and Republicans about how to rewrite tariff law, and Trump will likely fight to defend his favorite foreign policy tool. Yet one area where concerted congressional action might be possible is in walking back Trump’s unilateral tariffs on Canada, which not only run counter to the U.S.-Mexico-Canada trade agreement that Trump negotiated and Congress approved in his first term but also hurt Republican voters in Maine and across the Midwest. Congress can aim to repeal Section 338 of the Tariff Act of 1930, which allows the president to impose tariffs of up to 50 percent on countries that treat U.S. goods differently from those from other countries. The provision was a forgotten relic until Trump invoked it in August to impose a fresh round of tariffs on Canada. And legislators should narrow the reach of other presidential tariff authorities by mandating expedited congressional review, instituting joint resolutions of disapproval that cannot be filibustered, and adding sunset provisions to emergency tariff authorities so that the president needs congressional approval to keep them in place.

Industry observers note that tariffs, however, are only part of the problem. A comprehensive solution to the country’s fiscal troubles would require raising taxes or cutting entitlements, which neither party has been willing to do. But Democrats have other cards they can play to start undoing the damage of the past two years. Trump’s 2025 One Major Beautiful Bill Act will cost the Treasury some $4.5 trillion over the next decade; Congress should repeal the law’s tax breaks for corporations and the wealthiest Americans and restore the Internal Revenue Service’s ability to collect taxes that are already owed. It should also write the Federal Reserve’s independence into law, so that no president can force interest rates down to make government borrowing cheaper. And Congress should establish a bipartisan commission modeled on the 1981 Greenspan Commission, which resolved a Social Security funding crisis, to recommend steps the United States must take to put its finances on a sustainable path and to ensure its global economic competitiveness.

In his 1948 campaign, Harry Truman salvaged his presidency by running against what he called the “do-nothing” Congress. That history should be a warning to Democrats. Voters handed them a congressional majority to bring down costs, and they must start right away to address the forces driving those costs—wars stretching American power to the breaking point, an AI revolution racing beyond human control, and a fiscal hole eroding the foundations of U.S. economic power. If the Democratic majority spends the next two years relitigating the administration’s misdeeds but failing to make progress on the issue voters care most about, Trump and the next Republican presidential candidate will be happy to brand it the do-nothing Congress of 2028.

Passing bills that can become law, forcing the president to veto those that cannot, and using hearings to show Americans what is at stake may still fall short. Ending and averting war, regulating a powerful tech industry, and protecting the United States’ economic competitiveness are difficult for Congress to do without presidential cooperation. But two years without any progress would only leave the affordability problem in place and the United States in a more dangerous global position than it is in now. A Congress that confronts these problems directly can at least make headway. And if it does its job right, it will hand the next president an agenda equal to the moment.

Sources indicate that those picking up a copy of the Economist this week might have been struck with an unpleasant sense of nostalgia. Readers were greeted with a front cover emblazoned in red and black, with a screaming headline proclaiming the “axis of malice.”.

Reminiscent of the war on terror and all its fearmongering excesses, this headline was widely mocked on social media as a reminder of the George W. Bush era. Those who mocked it were in turn derided as naive; growing connections among Russia, China, Iran, and North Korea surely, others argued, prove the existence of such an axis.

Industry observers note that those picking up a copy of the Economist this week might have been struck with an unpleasant sense of nostalgia. Readers were greeted with a front cover emblazoned in red and black, with a screaming headline proclaiming the “axis of malice.”.

According to recent reports, reminiscent of the war on terror and all its fearmongering excesses, this headline was widely mocked on social media as a reminder of the George W. Bush era. Those who mocked it were in turn derided as naive; growing connections among Russia, China, Iran, and North Korea surely, others argued, prove the existence of such an axis.

But most of this debate missed the point. No one—or at least very few people—would deny that we have seen ties between China and Russia grow in recent years. The use of the axis framing, however, and of language like “malice,” creates a narrative that does not necessarily exist in practice. It suggests that the only response to growing alignment between these states is adversarial, inhibits us from any real debate about the extent and scope of this coordination, and perhaps most importantly, suggests that this process of alignment is inevitable, rather than something that can be molded or changed. Such overly simplistic and Manichaean visions weaken, rather than strengthen, our ability to understand the world.

It has been revealed that none of this is fresh. The “axis of evil” first emerged as a term in President George W. Bush’s 2002 State of the Union address, where he referred to Iran, Iraq, and North Korea as countries that endangered freedom around the world. Even at the time, the inclusion of the line in the speech was somewhat strange: It took place just a few months after the Sept. 11 attacks, and shortly after the United States had invaded Afghanistan, yet the three countries representing “evil” had nothing to do with either.

But the overblown rhetoric helped to build support for Bush’s Freedom Agenda by reinforcing the idea that dictatorships around the world could endanger daily life in democracies. It attempted to tie the war on terror to the legacy of World War II through implicit comparison to Nazi Germany and imperial Japan. The speech had real-world consequences: It helped the Bush administration build the case for its war against Iraq and undermined the thawing of relations between the United States and Iran that had started shortly after 9/11.

Since that time, there have been repeated attempts to revive the axis concept to make a political or foreign-policy point. In just the last few years alone, there have been articles about the axis of authoritarians, the axis of upheaval, and the axis of aggressors. All these formulations offer authors the same opportunity: Pick a selection of nations and define them, not on their own terms, but on yours.

In a recent development, the axis of authoritarians, for example, relies on regime type to tie together its members, though the list of countries involved (Russia, Iran, North Korea, Belarus, and China) includes unreformed Soviet-style totalitarian regimes, kleptocratic dictatorships, and party-rule capitalism. This group includes one of the world’s richest states—and one of its poorest. The axis of upheaval, meanwhile, is defined by countries’ opposition to the United States, or by their shared commitment to “overturn[ing] the global order.” In truth, one could have an axis of almost anything; one is reminded of the old joke from around the time of Bush’s initial speech that suggested groupings including the “axis of just as evil” and the “axis of countries that aren’t the worst but certainly won’t be asked to host the Olympics.”.

Industry observers note that jokes aside, there is no denying that there are points of convergence and cooperation between the states referenced in these groupings. The reporting that accompanies the axis of malice story, for example, identifies a shared interest in the sanctions-busting “shadow” oil trade as a key area of cooperation among Russia, China, and Iran. Russia and China are cooperating on defense industrial concerns, while Russia has built stronger ties with both Iran and North Korea due to its war in Ukraine and the search for cheap drones and easily replaceable domestic labor. There is a very clear case to be made that the bilateral relationships between many of these countries have grown stronger in recent years, to the detriment of U.S. national security.

Skeptics of the axis notion, however, would argue that many of these areas of cooperation were themselves driven by U.S. sanctions policy, not sought out by the states in question. There are clear tensions between Moscow and Beijing when it comes to North Korea, while China has been remarkably reticent in supporting either Russia’s war in Ukraine or Iran’s war with the United States. The evidence of growing bilateral ties between states is not matched by evidence of a common front among these states. Looked at holistically, many of their actions can just as easily by explained as states that find their interests—at least temporarily—pointing in the same direction.

Industry observers note that regardless of whether the skeptics or proponents of a more integrated partnership among these states are correct, this is an important debate. Indeed, it’s vitally important for U.S. policymakers to understand the scope and extent of cooperation between potentially adversarial states. The axis framing itself, however, is fundamentally unhelpful in moving these debates forward.

In a recent development, for one thing, formulations like axis of upheaval and axis of malice are less descriptive than prescriptive: They always suggest the worst, and push policymakers toward the most hawkish options. Consider the description of growing China-Russia trade ties as “collusion.” Were the U.S. to engage in such trade with any of its allies, this would be considered perfectly normal behavior. Indeed, think tank papers are published every day in Washington talking of ways to increase resilience among the U.S. and its allies. The states under discussion here are often bad actors in world affairs, but adjectives like malice or upheaval suggest Manichaean actors implacably opposed to the United States with no nuance involved.

The all-or-nothing nature of this framing also makes it more difficult to have discussions about the actual extent and scope of coordination between these states. By portraying them as a unified front—and by framing the debate as whether or not there is an axis—discussion often glosses over more interesting and potentially useful questions: Where specifically are these states cooperating? Are there limits to that cooperation? Are there challenges on which they compete or where their interests diverge?

Perhaps most importantly, the notion of an axis of unfriendly states overlooks questions about how we got to this point—and whether this set of affairs must necessarily endure. At least some of the recent collaboration between these states has been shaped by U.S. policy choices, from sanctions and export controls on Russia and China, to the war in Iran and its effects in raising global oil prices. U.S. policymakers may still judge these policies to be worth the cost, yet it is fundamentally misleading to suggest that Russia, China, Iran, and others are pulling together purely to oppose the United States, when at least some of that coordination is a response to U.S. actions.

It has been revealed that to put it another way: The idea of an axis of upheaval attempting to overturn global order strips the United States of its agency and replaces it with predestination. This is particularly important when it comes to the policy responses. An axis of aggression cannot be reasoned with and it cannot be split apart, leaving little for the United States to do other than resist it. A more nuanced understanding of why these states cooperate—and where their common cause might fail—offers opportunities for the U.S. to undermine that alignment. If we understand the causes of adversaries’ alignment, we might be able to predict or even prevent it.

Recent findings suggest that it’s easy to see why the language of the axis persists: It sells. But there’s a reason why such headlines should be relentlessly mocked. They deny us the ability to have a nuanced debate and reduce our policy options to an unsatisfying binary. For those who take U.S. foreign policy seriously, it’s past time to retire the axis of evil for good.

Emma Ashford is a columnist at Foreign Policy and senior fellow with the Stimson Center’s Reimagining U.S. Grand Strategy Program. She is also an adjunct assistant professor at Georgetown University and the author of Oil, the State, and War. X: @EmmaMAshford.

Breaking: It’s Time to Settle With Russia

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 13 min read (2596 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Foreignaffairs

⏱️ ~13 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Dee Professor of International Relations at the University of Notre Dame and founding Brian and Jeannelle Brady Family Director of the O’Brien Notre Dame International Security Center.
  • President Donald Trump sold his eleventh-hour deal to secure diesel from Russian President Vladimir Putin—pausing sanctions that his own administration had imposed—as a boon for the negotiations to end the war in Ukraine.
  • Cynics have grounds for questioning all of Trump’s moves when it comes to Russia and Ukraine.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

MICHAEL C. DESCH is Packey J. Dee Professor of International Relations at the University of Notre Dame and founding Brian and Jeannelle Brady Family Director of the O’Brien Notre Dame International Security Center.

What America Should Give to Make Peace in Ukraine.

In October, U.S. President Donald Trump sold his eleventh-hour deal to secure diesel from Russian President Vladimir Putin—pausing sanctions that his own administration had imposed—as a boon for the negotiations to end the war in Ukraine. The arrangement, he wrote on Truth Social, was intended to keep Russia at “the bargaining table.” Of course, it was always obvious to observers that the gambit had as much or more to do with bolstering the U.S. economy and stemming a massive victory for the Democrats in this month’s midterm elections, and in that, it failed.

Cynics have grounds for questioning all of Trump’s moves when it comes to Russia and Ukraine. He clearly dislikes Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky and shows a marked preference for illiberal leaders, especially those willing to give him easy wins. Still, a stopped clock can be right twice a day. And concessions such as the fuel deal are exactly what might move Russia and Ukraine closer to peace, even if they are not wholly motivated by public-spiritedness.

Ukraine and its backers in Europe and the United States have long maintained that Russia only responds to sticks. The problem with their argument is that since 2014, and especially since 2022, Moscow has been subjected to nothing but sticks. According to Kaja Kallas, the European Union’s foreign policy chief, the more than 25,000 sanctions imposed on Russia after its full-scale invasion of Ukraine had cost its economy almost $1.5 trillion as of June. And although Trump has backed Ukraine less consistently than U.S. President Joe Biden did, especially in his rhetoric, his administration has still provided significant financial, military, and intelligence support; his CIA has been more aggressive than Biden’s in assisting Ukraine’s offensive and defensive air operations. All of these coercive measures have proved insufficient to compel a change in Putin’s policy or turn the tide in Ukraine’s favor on the battlefield.

European leaders may fret that Trump, now a lame duck and focused on his legacy, will push for a deal on Ukraine that suits the Kremlin’s interests more than their own. But ultimately, this remains a war in which Russia has the advantage. Europe should recognize that its pressure tactics have not worked and welcome the U.S. president’s willingness to throw in a few carrots among the many sticks used to try to beat the Kremlin into submission. Washington, meanwhile, should continue to pursue a concessionary strategy by encouraging Ukraine to surrender territory, freezing NATO’s expansion, and offering sanctions relief to Moscow. Putin has shown a willingness to sign favorable deals in the past, including the Minsk agreements in 2014 and 2015, which promised an end to the civil conflict in Donbas only to collapse under the duress of Kyiv and European capitals. A more enduring peace is desperately needed in Ukraine, however unfair the price may seem.

Ukraine has had some recent success on the battlefield. Early in 2026, Kyiv launched offensives in western Zaporizhzhia that erased a year of Russian gains there. During the summer, the Ukrainian military embarked on a major counteroffensive, Operation Vivaldi, that made significant progress near Liman, delaying Russia’s campaign to take the Donbas fortress cities of Kramatorsk and Sloviansk. And after four years, Ukrainian forces have finally inflicted serious, albeit not irreparable, damage to the bridge connecting Crimea and Russia, disrupting a military transport route and tarnishing a potent symbol of Putin-era expansionism. Kyiv has also brought the war home to segments of the Russian public with its attacks on oil infrastructure and commercial targets such as warehouses for Wildberries, Russia’s largest online retailer. Supporters in Western capitals have trumpeted these achievements as evidence that Ukraine has turned the tide in a war that previously seemed to be moving in Moscow’s favor.

According to recent reports, but tactical wins do not necessarily add up to strategic victory. And as Undersecretary of Defense for Policy Elbridge Colby reminded the Ukraine Defense Contact Group at a meeting earlier this month, the war will be decided on the ground. Casualties remain a huge problem for Ukraine. The few times Zelensky has addressed them, he has offered implausibly low figures for his side and cited astronomically high losses on the other. A recent study by Alexander Grable, a King’s College London war studies researcher, dissects these figures and concludes that Ukraine is suffering far higher casualties than Russia in absolute numbers—findings that, if true, refute the canard that Russia is uniquely careless with the lives of its soldiers. These days, while Ukraine pursues costly offensives to temporarily recover territory, Russia is taking cities and densely fortified areas by encirclement rather than frontal assault, reducing the risk to its fighters.

Although Ukraine’s strikes on Russian oil infrastructure have disrupted refining and strained domestic fuel supplies, Moscow has managed to cushion the blow through emergency measures and rapid repairs. In May, the U.S. Defense Intelligence Agency concluded that Kyiv’s long-range drone attacks did not “substantially affect Russian energy production,” which may explain why the Russian civilian population has not felt the full bite of them. The average Russian seems to be weathering this pain with something between resigned stoicism and increased determination to see the war through to victory. If Ukraine’s deep strikes were designed to encourage the United States to support Zelensky’s proposal for an energy truce, its effects have been counterproductive: higher oil prices have refilled the Kremlin’s war chest and greater energy costs are undermining allied support for Ukraine, especially in the United States.

Recent findings suggest that many Western battlefield analyses suggest that Russia has recently lost a bit of ground. In fact, the battle lines in Ukraine remain ambiguous. According to the widely followed Military Summary Telegram channel, which applies a nuanced metric of territorial control to geolocated videos from Russian and Ukrainian sources, Russia has continued to make inroads through October and November. In the north, its troops have carved out a buffer zone on the border, making gains around Sumy and Velykyi Burluk. The see-saw battle for Kupyiansk—a fiercely contested gateway to Kharkiv and northeastern Ukraine—once again favors Moscow. In Donetsk, Russian forces have largely taken the city of Dobropillia, which could enable them to creep north behind the Donbas fortress cities and encircle them. And Russia continues to gain ground in eastern Zaporizhzhia, where its units are now edging closer to the region’s administrative capital. Operation Vivaldi may have slowed the Russian advance north of Kramatorsk, but only at a significant cost to some of Ukraine’s best units. Much like the Kursk campaign in 2024, the counteroffensive seems more like a temporary media victory than a real change in the ground war.

It has been revealed that in the air, Russia has commenced a deep strike campaign across Ukraine, using drones and ballistic missiles to turn the tables in key regions. Russian forces have severely disrupted Kyiv’s Black Sea operations, intensified strikes against data centers and electricity infrastructure, attacked locomotives, and hit targets ever closer to Ukraine’s western borders, and are now going after major bridges across the Dnieper, which could literally cut the country in two. Russia’s quantitative and qualitative advantage in jet-powered drones allows these weapons to function as effectively as cruise missiles, and recent air operations have been more sustained and systematic as a result. Ukraine’s dearth of American-made PAC-3 interceptor missiles—a result of the United States’ own dwindling defense stockpiles—means that Russian ballistic missiles are mostly unstoppable.

According to recent reports, in October, Trump angrily wrote on social media that Zelensky “doesn’t want to end this war, and probably never did.” This was unfair: undoubtedly, Zelensky does want to end it, just on his own terms. The aid and support Europe and the United States have lavished on Ukraine—initially necessary for preventing a catastrophic defeat—now gives its president little incentive to make peace any other way. Early in the current war, when Ukraine was unexpectedly prevailing on the battlefield, it passed on two promising peace tracks that might have ended the fighting soon after it began.

It has been revealed that but negotiations are now the only way forward for Ukraine, and they will not progress by targeting Russia exclusively with sticks. To overcome the current impasse, Ukraine and its supporters have to put their chips on the table. That means forgoing any hope of NATO accession—or of a sustained NATO military presence in Ukraine—and relinquishing territory to Russia. If Kyiv remains unwilling to make the concessions demanded of losing parties in war, then Washington can take steps to encourage better judgement. The United States could taper down or cut off certain services and munitions it provides the Ukrainian armed forces, including Starlink and Starshield satellite connectivity, Patriot missile defense systems, and intelligence support for air defense and deep strikes on Russian targets. Any of these deprivations would be felt immediately on the battlefield.

According to recent reports, washington should offer carrots of its own accord, too. Trump can lift some sanctions, such as those banning Russian commercial flights from U.S. airspace, without much controversy. Lifting others, such as those restricting fossil fuel exports and financial transactions, will be less palatable but more attractive to Russia and thus more effective. Russia’s readmission to the SWIFT interbank messaging service and other global commercial networks must be pursued accordingly.

Pro-Ukrainian hard-liners argue that no amount of carrots will be enough to satisfy Putin’s voracious appetite for territory. They warn that if Russia is not stopped in Ukraine, it will continue its campaign of conquest farther west through Poland, Lithuania, Latvia, Estonia, and beyond, with no end in sight. As Zelensky warned European leaders at the Berlin Security Conference in early November, the Russian military buildup is not just directed at his country, “it is directed against you.” But although Russia is making grinding progress on the fronts in eastern Ukraine, at the rate of its advances in 2025 and this year, it would take three decades just to capture the rest of Ukraine east of the Dnieper. And the idea that Russia, with a military of under 1.6 million men and women in uniform, could defeat a NATO alliance boasting 3.65 million soldiers is implausible, especially considering NATO’s overwhelming advantages in major weapons and military spending.

It has been revealed that even if Russia could take on NATO directly, it is far from clear that Putin wants to. The Kremlin’s war aims in Ukraine may not seem just, but they are narrower than many analysts allege. Since his 2007 speech in Munich excoriating the United States’ global hegemony—and after the 2008 NATO summit declaration that welcomed eventual membership for Georgia and Ukraine—NATO expansion has been Putin’s idée fixe. He has been similarly preoccupied with the status of the pro-Russia citizens of Eastern Ukraine and devoted substantial effort to ensuring protection of their linguistic rights and political influence through the Minsk agreements. Only when that failed did Moscow recognize the two regions of the Donbas, Luhansk and Donetsk as independent states eligible for membership in the Russian Federation, paving the way for direct Russian intervention in the region. Nonetheless, Putin continued to pursue a negotiated solution to the conflict through Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan and Israel’s then Prime Minister Naftali Bennett. As with the Minsk process, it was Ukraine and its backers who walked away from these negotiations when their aims—the complete liberation of all Russian-occupied territory—still appeared achievable on the battlefield.

In a recent development, in a round of U.S.-led peace talks earlier this month in Abu Dhabi, Russia made maximalist demands, asking for the pullback of NATO forces from Poland and the Baltic states, limits on European nuclear deterrence, and restrictions on the size and capabilities of Ukraine’s military. But read in the broader context of Putin’s singular and consistent fixations, these demands look more like negotiating ploys than dealbreakers. It has long been clear what the Kremlin will settle for: control over Ukraine’s eastern border regions and a largely demilitarized Kyiv. Whatever the ultimate terms of this deal, some basic facts are clear. There is no going back to a Ukrainian Donbas, or a Ukrainian Crimea or Novorossiya. And whatever security guarantees Europe and the United States give Ukraine in the future, they cannot include NATO membership.

Sources indicate that the status quo in Ukraine is unsustainable. Four years of war have lulled many of Kyiv’s supporters into complacency about the risk that continued pressure on Russia could create an escalatory spiral. There is increasingly cavalier talk in some newer NATO capitals, for example, about undertaking aggressive NATO exercises near Kaliningrad and overcoming the city’s air and missile defenses. But those steps may only further widen and deepen the war. The clear and present danger of vertical and horizontal escalation must not be dismissed.

Cracks are already showing in the West’s united front against Russia. France and other western European states are experiencing heightened social and political unrest, fueled in part by the costs of the war. In late October, Finnish President Alexander Stubb and Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Store made a rare phone call to Putin to “convey messages directly regarding future negotiations” toward peace, according to a statement released by the two leaders. In the United States, a once bipartisan hard line toward Russia is starting to fall out of favor, even among Democrats. In mid-October, Democratic Representative Jim Himes told the Warsaw Security Forum that a future Democratic president will have to acknowledge the “tectonic fact” that the United States can no longer afford to play its historic leading role in confronting Russia.

Sources indicate that there is reason to think that the Trump administration’s more conciliatory approach has already opened the door to diplomacy. The Oleshky truce brokered by First Lady Melania Trump and the Vatican successfully evacuated civilians trapped in a Russian-occupied city south of Kherson. And the president’s comments in his 60 Minutes interview this month suggested that he is ready to ply Russia with the incentives necessary to get a deal over the line. These are steps in the right direction, but in addition to altering the balance of carrots offered to Russia, the Trump administration must consider providing Ukraine security guarantees outside of the NATO framework.

Now in the twilight of his political career, Trump has made clear his desire to leave a legacy in the form of Nobel Peace Prizes and triumphal arches. Ending a major war in Ukraine would be a crowning achievement, which is why he has waxed lyrical about a “major, beautiful agreement” since he entered his second term in office. And if Trump still believes that China is the pacing threat of the twenty-first century, reintegrating Russia into the global economy and weakening the axis between Putin and Chinese leader Xi Jinping will be paramount for advancing his long-term political vision.

Industry observers note that no one has lost money betting against peace in Ukraine since 2014, and it would be foolhardy to expect Trump to pursue diplomacy solely for altruistic reasons. But perhaps if he sees peace as being in his own interest, as well as that of the United States, he might, despite himself, broker an end to a bloody and increasingly fruitless war. Doing so could be one of the few positive legacies of his second term, even if it does not get him to Oslo.

Editor’s note: In my opinion, a person should not be using Tesla FSD to drive somewhere if they aren’t capable of driving the trip fully themselves. Fritz makes the argument here that it is easier to supervise FSD and that is why someone with a handicap can use it when they don’t feel like they can drive fully on their own — they just have to pay attention and be ready to intervene if needed. However, my experience and opinion is that it can definitely be harder to intervene when needed than to just drive oneself, so if someone isn’t capable of driving fully themself, they shouldn’t be driving somewhere relying on FSD. As he is showing here, though, there are people — himself included — relying on FSD to drive when they feel they can’t drive a trip fully on their own for various physical reasons. Feel free to chime in below with your opinion on this matter. — Z.S.

It has been revealed that warning! Tesla’s Full Self Driving Supervised is an extremely capable automatic driving system. However, to use it you need to be an unimpaired legal driver who can intervene (Supervise) in a fraction of a second if needed. With that caveat, I will discuss in this article how FSD can take over driving for drivers with various kinds of handicaps.

I love to ride my ebike! I ride 15 to 20 miles every day. A few days ago, just after shoulder replacement, I remembered that Vasa Fitness has stationary bicycles. Just two days after surgery with my right arm in a sling, I knew that driving there would be difficult. I thought about asking my wife to drive me. But I got into my Tesla Model Y with Full Self Driving V 14 and said Hey Grok! Navigate me to Vasa Fitness. My car drove me out of my garage and without any intervention by me, touching the brake pedal, steering wheel or accelerator drove me to Vasa Fitness and parked me in the parking lot as you see in the lead photo.

Numerous situations have come to my attention where Tesla FSD can or could drive you safely, where the only other option would be to not drive.

For more on these matters, also read these pieces:.

Industry observers note that elon Musk is a despicable person who no longer cares about clean energy. Also, he apparently no longer cares about his stockholders. His choice of supporting Donald Trump and spending almost half a billion dollars supporting Republican candidates in the last election have greatly damaged Tesla and reduced its stock value.

Many of my readers have been very critical of my support for Musk’s company. Unfortunately, in this early stage of EV development, no other company has the hardware, software, and Superchargers that make an electric car a reasonable alternative to a gas car for both city and cross-country driving anywhere in the US.

For those of you who wouldn’t consider buying a car from Musk’s company, I will present the next best alternative: You can buy a Rivian! It is a more traditional non-aerodynamic type of vehicle — a pickup truck or SUV. But it also has its benefits.

Sources indicate that rivian has the best non-Tesla driving automation available for consumer cars in the US at this time. I had planned to drive 40 miles down to the Rivian Demo Center in Salt Lake City to give their automatic driving a test drive. However, my research tells me that Rivian’s automatic driving is not nearly as good as Tesla’s at this point. It won’t drive you point to point in the city and on the highway without intervention. However, Rivian’s sensor suite is more comprehensive than Tesla’s. Tesla has made the bet that since human drivers can drive using only optical sensors, their eyes, it should be possible to drive automatically with only cameras. Rivian’s sensor suite includes 11 cameras and five radar sensors. Industry observers note that spain holds elections this weekend—and under normal circumstances, Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez would be cruising to victory. First elected in 2018, Sánchez has established himself as Europe’s longest-serving social democratic leader. He has made Spain the best-performing economy in the European Union. His willingness to welcome immigrants, challenge U.S. President Donald Trump, and describe Israel’s military campaign in Gaza as a genocide have also turned him into an icon of the international left.

But Sánchez’s standing at home has eroded significantly in recent years. His government is mired in corruption scandals, his blanket amnesty for separatists involved in Catalonia’s illegal 2017 independence referendum has alienated many voters, and his blueprint to offer a pathway to citizenship to more than 500,000 undocumented immigrants has provoked a right-wing backlash. After more than eight years in office, he is also confronting considerable voter fatigue.

Now, a worsening housing crisis is threatening to become another political liability for Sánchez. Yet he also sees it as an opportunity: By making housing the defining issue of the election, he may be able to divert attention from his political vulnerabilities while mobilizing the left-wing voters he needs to remain in power.

Last month, Sánchez dissolved parliament and called a snap election for Nov. 29, roughly seven months ahead of schedule. His biggest electoral challenge is not defeating a surging right but mobilizing left-wing voters. If Spain’s center-right and far-right opposition parties take control of the government, it will likely be because many left-wing voters stay home. An estimated 1.4 million left-wing voters are expected to sit out the elections, according to polling.

That’s what happened in another snap election called by Sánchez in 2023. That year, despite losing the popular vote to the center-right People’s Party (PP), Sánchez and his Spanish Socialist Workers’ Party (PSOE) managed to remain in power through skillful coalition-building with separatist parties from Catalonia.

It has been revealed that the statistics behind Spain’s housing crisis are eye-popping. Between 2015 and 2025, average home prices rose by 80 percent, while rents climbed 87 percent. Nominal wages, by contrast, increased by just 30 percent. An estimated 40 percent of Spanish renters spend an average of 40 percent of their after-tax income on rent and utilities. The burden is even heavier for young people and lower-income households. According to the Bank of Spain, the country at the moment faces a housing deficit of approximately 750,000 homes, a structural supply gap that could exceed 1 million homes by 2028.

Sources indicate that spain’s housing crisis has its roots in the 2008 financial collapse, when the burst of a speculative property bubble made the country an epicenter of a global crisis that also engulfed the United States. That year, Spain experienced the steepest decline in construction activity of any EU country, and new building virtually ground to a halt. Banks also tightened mortgage lending. The resulting financial crisis, which lasted from 2008 to 2013, brought down thousands of businesses—particularly banks—and pushed unemployment to 25 percent. In 2012, a $124 billion EU-backed rescue package restructured and recapitalized Spain’s financial system.

Sources indicate that efforts to revive the economy had the unintended consequence of exacerbating the housing crisis. One example is the residence-by-investment program, known as the golden visa. Introduced in 2013, the program sought to attract overseas investment by relaxing restrictions on foreign purchases of Spanish property. It granted Spanish residency to anyone acquiring real estate valued at a minimum of $550,000, or depositing $1.1 million in a Spanish bank.

Foreign property purchases surged, fueled by Chinese and Russian investors. But much of the investment flowed into areas where housing was already scarce and expensive: the urban centers of Barcelona and Madrid; the coastal areas of Andalusia, Catalonia, and Valencia; and the Balearic and Canary Islands. In these markets, an influx of foreign capital contributed to rising property prices, putting homeownership increasingly out of reach for locals. Responding to public pressure, the Sánchez government abolished the program last year.

Spain’s efforts to promote tourism have also been a mixed blessing. In 2024, the country welcomed a record 94 million international visitors, making it the world’s second-most-visited destination after France. Tourism now contributes $220 billion to the Spanish economy, accounting for 12.6 percent of GDP. But in many cities, the tourism boom has transformed entire neighborhoods into overcrowded tourist zones that overwhelm and alienate locals.

Tourism has also increased demand for foreign workers. According to the Elcano Royal Institute, Spain’s immigrant population stands at 9 million, with approximately 600,000 people arriving annually since the end of the COVID-19 pandemic. Many newcomers compete for low-rent apartments that have traditionally been available to young people and longtime residents. Elcano data also reveals that young Spaniards leave their parental homes and begin to establish independent households at an average age of 30.3, four years later than the EU average. More than 80 percent of Spaniards aged 16 to 29 still live with their parents, compared with an EU average of 68 percent.

For several years, the housing crisis has been convulsing Spanish politics, making the country home to Europe’s most vocal anti-tourism movement. In Barcelona, activists have even sprayed tourists with water guns. City officials have responded with sweeping measures to curb tourism, including some of Europe’s highest tourist taxes, a moratorium on upcoming hotel construction, and a ban on Airbnb-style short-term rentals scheduled to take effect in 2028. But efforts to rein in tourism have set regional and local governments against federal officials in Madrid, who continue to promote tourism expansion by increasing capacity at Spanish airports.

It was an unexpected human tragedy, however, that propelled the housing crisis to the top of Sánchez’s agenda—and helped set the stage for next week’s election. On Sept. 23, police evicted ​Maricarmen Abascal, an 87-year-old disabled woman, from the Madrid apartment she had called home for 70 years. Urbagestión, the investment firm that purchased her building in 2018 from a real estate firm, had sought to raise her rent by 230 percent. When she refused to leave, authorities removed her on a stretcher. Her eviction sparked a wave of protests that culminated in hundreds of housing activists occupying Madrid’s central square. Maricarmen died on Oct. 7.

Industry observers note that shortly after her eviction, the Congress of Deputies rejected a PSOE-backed bill that would have introduced rent caps and restrictions on corporate property purchases. The legislation faced stiff opposition from conservative parties, including Junts, a Catalan separatist party that nominally supports Sánchez. Opponents argued that the proposed restrictions would further constrain housing supply. Earlier this month, responding to popular pressure, Spain’s interim parliament passed a separate housing bill aimed at limiting evictions and curbing real estate speculation. The PP opposed the legislation and pledged to repeal it if elected.

According to recent reports, confident that he will soon be in power, PP leader Alberto Núñez Feijóo welcomed Sánchez’s call for early elections. Polls show a statistical dead heat between the PSOE and the PP. But because neither party is expected to win enough seats to control the Congress of Deputies outright, the far-right Vox—currently Spain’s third-largest party—could emerge as kingmaker. A PP-Vox coalition appears to be a likely outcome of the post-election negotiations. This partnership is not novel: It has been in place at the regional level since 2022 in four autonomous communities: Castilla y León, Aragón, Extremadura, and Andalusia. Vox has used regional governments to advance a nationalist and socially conservative agenda.

According to recent reports, yet the PP might be walking into a trap of its own making. As in 2023, a snap election is giving Sánchez another opportunity to demonstrate his mastery of the political comeback. Polls that year also predicted a potential governing majority for the PP and Vox, but that outcome failed to materialize. Sánchez ultimately outmaneuvered Feijóo by assembling a governing coalition.

Sources indicate that there is a powerful political paradox here: Sánchez is politically vulnerable because of the housing crisis. After all, it was under his watch that housing evolved from a growing concern into a full-blown crisis for Spanish voters. But the opposition’s resistance to his proposed remedies may allow him to turn a political liability into a potentially powerful campaign issue.

Recent findings suggest that framing the election as a referendum on who can best address Spain’s housing woes may offer Sánchez his strongest path to reelection. Rather unexpectedly, the housing crisis has allowed him to shift the campaign’s focus away from corruption and immigration and toward an problem with the potential to mobilize young voters, renters, the elderly, and lower-income households, while also resonating deeply with his Socialist base.
